name: Passkeys, WebAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth
tagline: Replace shared secrets and phishable OTPs with origin-bound asymmetric cryptography stored in hardware enclaves.
purpose: Understand how WebAuthn registration and assertion ceremonies work, why origin binding defeats phishing proxies, and how to handle signCount cloning and multi-device passkey recovery.

spark.summary: WebAuthn/FIDO2 replaces passwords with per-site asymmetric keypairs generated inside a user's hardware authenticator, where private keys never leave the device and signatures are cryptographically bound to the exact Relying Party origin.
spark.keyTakeaway: When untrusted callers cross a trust boundary, webAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth, because the browser—not the user—supplies the verified origin into the signed challenge, even a pixel-perfect reverse-proxy phishing site cannot replay a WebAuthn assertion.
spark.byteSummary:
Traditional passwords and SMS/TOTP one-time codes are shared secrets: if a user is tricked into typing them into an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing proxy, the attacker replays the credentials against the real site in real time. WebAuthn and FIDO2 eliminate shared secrets by using per-site asymmetric keypairs (typically ES256 / P-256 or Ed25519) anchored in a hardware Secure Enclave, TPM, or roaming security key.

During registration (`navigator.credentials.create()`), the Relying Party (RP) server issues a fresh cryptographic challenge and its `rpId` (e.g., `app.example.com`). The authenticator verifies user presence/biometrics locally, generates a unique keypair scoped to that `rpId`, retains the private key inside hardware, and returns the public key and `credentialId` to the server.

During authentication (`navigator.credentials.get()`), the server sends a one-time random challenge; the browser constructs `clientDataJSON` containing the exact active TLS origin, and the authenticator signs `sha256(authenticatorData) || sha256(clientDataJSON)`. Because the signature binds both the server challenge and the browser-verified origin, a phishing domain like `app-example.com` produces an invalid signature that the real RP immediately rejects.

Key trade-offs and failure modes: synced passkeys (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager) solve device-loss lockouts via end-to-end encrypted key sync, but often report `signCount = 0` rather than monotonically incrementing counters—so servers must not blindly reject `signCount == 0` when `backupEligible` is set. Servers must also enforce single-use challenge TTLs and strict `rpIdHash` checks.

learningJourney.title: Why Passwords and TOTP Fail Against Reverse-Proxy Phishing
learningJourney.purpose: Establish why shared-secret MFA cannot stop real-time adversary-in-the-middle proxies, whereas origin-bound signatures do.

explanation.foundation: Even with 6-digit TOTP or SMS codes, an **Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM)** reverse proxy sits between the victim and the legitimate login page, forwarding the username, password, and OTP in real time and stealing the resulting session cookie.
explanation.core: FIDO2/WebAuthn defeats AiTM phishing because **the browser enforces origin binding**: the authenticator signs the TLS origin observed by the browser (`https://evil-login.com`), which never matches the legitimate Relying Party's expected origin (`https://example.com`).
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of Passkeys, WebAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth, watch how why passwords and totp fail against reverse-proxy phishing interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. Deep-dive into FIDO2/WebAuthn attestation, `authenticatorData` bitflags (`UP`/`UV`/`BE`/`BS`), atomic challenge consumption, and `rpId` scoping.

learningJourney.title: The WebAuthn Registration Ceremony (Attestation)
learningJourney.purpose: Trace how a Relying Party issues a challenge and persists a scoped public key without ever seeing a private key.

explanation.core: **Server Challenge**: RP generates a 32-byte CSPRNG `challenge`, stores it in short-lived state (e.g., Redis with 5-minute TTL), and specifies `rp.id`, `user.id`, and allowed algorithms (`-7` ES256, `-8` EdDSA). 2. **Browser & Authenticator**: `navigator.credentials.create()` invokes the platform authenticator (Touch ID, Windows Hello, Android Biometrics) or roaming key.
explanation.deepDive: 3. **Server Verification**: RP verifies the challenge matches and has not expired, validates `rpIdHash == sha256(rp.id)`, checks `UP` (User Present) and `UV` (User Verified) flags, and stores `(credentialId, publicKey, signCount)`.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Passkeys, WebAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: When untrusted callers cross a trust boundary, webAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth, because the browser—not the user—supplies the verified origin into the signed challenge, even a pixel-perfect reverse-proxy phishing site cannot replay a WebAuthn assertion.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

learningJourney.title: Assertion Verification, Origin Binding & Replay Protection
learningJourney.purpose: Walk through every cryptographic check the server must perform on a WebAuthn login assertion.

explanation.core:
The RP server **must** verify all of the following in order:
- **Challenge**: `clientDataJSON.challenge` matches the stored single-use challenge (and delete it immediately to prevent replay).
- **Origin & Type**: `clientDataJSON.type === 'webauthn.get'` and `clientDataJSON.origin` matches your exact allowlisted HTTPS origin.
- **RP ID Hash**: First 32 bytes of `authenticatorData` equal `sha256(expectedRpId)`.
- **Signature**: Verify `signature` over `authenticatorData || sha256(clientDataJSON)` using the stored COSE public key.
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of Passkeys, WebAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth, watch how assertion verification, origin binding & replay protection interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. Deep-dive into FIDO2/WebAuthn attestation, `authenticatorData` bitflags (`UP`/`UV`/`BE`/`BS`), atomic challenge consumption, and `rpId` scoping.

learningJourney.title: Resident (Discoverable) Keys vs. Enterprise Hardware Keys
learningJourney.purpose: Compare cloud-synced passkeys and hardware-bound FIDO2 keys across recovery, UX, and enterprise attestation.

explanation.foundation: - **Synced Passkeys (Multi-Device)**: Stored in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, or 1Password; `BE` (Backup Eligible) and `BS` (Backed Up) flags are `1`.
explanation.core: Great for consumer UX because losing a phone does not lock out the account. - **Device-Bound Keys (Single-Device)**: YubiKeys or enterprise TPMs where `BE=0`.
explanation.deepDive: Required for high-assurance government/fintech compliance where keys must never leave physical hardware.

learningJourney.title: Preventing Lockout Without Weakening Security
learningJourney.purpose: Design multi-passkey enrollment and high-assurance recovery flows so fallback channels do not become the weakest link.

explanation.foundation: If a user registers a single hardware key and loses it, falling back to an unverified SMS reset reintroduces SIM-swap risk.
explanation.core:
Best practices:
1. Encourage **2+ passkeys** (e.g., platform passkey + backup security key or synced password manager).
2. Use **WebAuthn Conditional UI** (`mediation: 'conditional'`) for one-tap autofill login.
3. Gate recovery with **high-entropy recovery codes** or identity-verified re-enrollment delays.
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of Passkeys, WebAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth, watch how preventing lockout without weakening security interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. Deep-dive into FIDO2/WebAuthn attestation, `authenticatorData` bitflags (`UP`/`UV`/`BE`/`BS`), atomic challenge consumption, and `rpId` scoping.

learningJourney.title: Subdomain rpId Scope, signCount=0 False Positives & Browser Quirks
learningJourney.purpose: Avoid common production outages caused by misconfigured rpId domains or naive signCount checks.

explanation.foundation: - **`rpId` Domain Mismatch**: Setting `rpId` to `login.example.com` prevents credentials from working on `app.example.com`.
explanation.core: Use the registrable domain (`example.com`) if passkeys span subdomains—but never a public suffix. - **False Cloned-Key Lockouts**: Multi-device synced passkeys intentionally emit `signCount = 0`.
explanation.deepDive: Always check `stored_count > 0 && new_count > 0` before flagging a clone.

beginner.summary: Passkeys replace passwords with a private key stored safely on your device and a public key saved on the website.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When untrusted callers cross a trust boundary, WebAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth, because the browser—not the user—supplies the verified origin into the signed challenge, even a pixel-perfect reverse-proxy phishing site cannot replay a WebAuthn assertion.
beginner.byteSummary:
Instead of typing a password that can be guessed or phished, passkeys use a pair of cryptographic keys. Your phone or laptop keeps the private key locked behind your fingerprint or face, while the website only stores the public key.

When you log in, the browser includes the real website address in what gets signed. Even if a scammer builds a lookalike website, the signature won't match the real site.

intermediate.summary: WebAuthn/FIDO2 uses hardware-backed asymmetric keys and browser-enforced origin binding (`clientDataJSON` + `rpIdHash`) to defeat AiTM phishing.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When untrusted callers cross a trust boundary, WebAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth, because the browser—not the user—supplies the verified origin into the signed challenge, even a pixel-perfect reverse-proxy phishing site cannot replay a WebAuthn assertion.
intermediate.byteSummary:
During registration, the Relying Party issues a CSPRNG challenge and `rpId`, and the authenticator generates a scoped keypair inside its Secure Enclave/TPM. During login, the authenticator signs `authenticatorData || sha256(clientDataJSON)`.

Because the browser injects the real TLS origin into `clientDataJSON`, AiTM phishing proxies cannot replay assertions. Production backends must consume challenges atomically (`GETDEL`) and exempt `signCount == 0` for cloud-synced passkeys.

advanced.summary: Deep-dive into FIDO2/WebAuthn attestation, `authenticatorData` bitflags (`UP`/`UV`/`BE`/`BS`), atomic challenge consumption, and `rpId` scoping.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When untrusted callers cross a trust boundary, WebAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth, because the browser—not the user—supplies the verified origin into the signed challenge, even a pixel-perfect reverse-proxy phishing site cannot replay a WebAuthn assertion.
advanced.byteSummary:
WebAuthn binds assertions to `sha256(rpId)` and browser-asserted `clientDataJSON.origin`, eliminating credential replay across lookalike domains. Registration stores `(credentialId, COSE_key, signCount, BE/BS)`.

On assertion, servers must atomically consume the 32-byte challenge, verify `UP`/`UV` flags per policy, validate the COSE signature over `authenticatorData || sha256(clientDataJSON)`, and only flag cloning when `stored_count > 0 && new_count > 0 && new_count <= stored_count`.
